title: Asymmetric expert load signal decomposition and mitigation notes
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an investigation into recurring asymmetric expert load patterns we observed on long-context MoE workloads (mostly Qwen-XXL and a Llama-based MoE variant) running on our dedicated clusters. Goal is to decompose the observable signal into root causes (routing hotness, tokenization skew, KV cache warmup, and backend IO), document reproducible traces, and propose short/medium-term mitigations that are cheap to try in the runtime.

Summary of the observed problem:
- Intermittent p99 latency spikes (~2-3x baseline) for requests to MoE model endpoints when context lengths exceed ~8k tokens.
- These spikes correlate with high variance in per-expert queue lengths: small subset of experts receives 60–80% of routed tokens for bursts, while others remain idle.
- Spikes are more frequent on Qwen-XXL experiments than on the Mistral-MoE prototype, suggesting architecture + tokenizer interaction.
- Affected requests are often multi-turn user sessions that append long system/context windows; single-shot short prompts rarely trigger the pattern.

Repro methodology:
- Synthetic replay harness: We replay production traces (anonymized) at 1x, 2x, and 5x scale against a canary pool. Replay includes authentic tokenization and session chunking.
- Instrumentation: added per-expert enqueue/dequeue counters, per-request routing histogram, NVTX annotated kernels (attn, ffn, router), and a lightweight PCIe/DRAM evictions counter collected from node metrics.
- Platforms: tests run on p4d/8xA100-like machine images used in Dedicated (same kernel, same driver), and on smaller 4xA100 dev boxes for quicker iterations.

Key traces / signals found:
1) Routing hotness vs token-position:
   - Hot experts receive disproportionate tokens early in the generation window (first ~2k tokens of a long session). After ~2k tokens, distribution smooths slightly but remains skewed.
   - Hypothesis: prefix patterns in prompt/designated roles cause expert gating to collapse to a few experts (content-aligned bias).

2) KV cache warmup and memory pressure:
   - When skew occurs, those experts' KV shards are accessed frequently and cause repeated GPU memory page faults when we rely on UVM or when we have multi-model packing on a single GPU. Pagefault bursts precede latency spikes by ~100–300ms in traces.
   - On setups with strict OOM prevention (eager eviction), we see increased PCIe throughput coincident with the hot period.

3) Scheduling/serialization of expert kernels:
   - Because only a few experts are hot, the runtime serializes many expert calls on small subsets of SMs, increasing kernel contention. This shows up as a sustained rise in kernel queue depth and longer kernel duration variance.

4) Tokenization aliasing and session-level patterns:
   - Token streams that contain certain repeated delimiter tokens in the prefix (observed in customer traces) strongly correlate with mapping to the same gating subset. Tokenizer differences across models are significant: Qwen tokenization produced longer sparse substring matches that bias gating compared to Llama tokenizer.

Microbenchmarks we ran:
- Synthetic uniform content vs production-like skewed content: uniform content produces near-even expert load and stable 95th pctl latencies. Production-like content reproduces the skew and the p99 spikes.
- Controlled prefix substitution: replacing the first 512 tokens with neutral tokens reduced early-hotness by ~40% and reduced p99 by ~25%.
- KV cache pinned vs unpinned: pinning frequently-used shards eliminated pagefault spikes but increased steady-state memory usage by ~15%.

Immediate hypotheses (ranked by likelihood):
A) Gating function is content-sensitive and certain token sequences act as high-confidence triggers mapping to specific expert indices.
B) Tokenization differences across models (Qwen vs Llama/Mistral) amplify gating hotspots because subword fragments create repeated high-probability pathways.
C) Runtime memory reclamation/eviction policy combined with skew causes repeated UVM/pagefault churn on hot shards.
D) Scheduling favors co-located experts (topology-aware placement) which backfires when those co-located experts are hot, creating localized SM saturation.

Short-term mitigations to try (cheap, non-invasive):
1) Prefetch-on-route: when an expert receives >X routed tokens within Y ms for the same session, proactively prefetch/commit its KV shard to GPU memory for the next M steps. (Configurable thresholds; aim to reduce pagefaults.)
2) Randomized gate jitter: add a tiny stochastic noise to gating logits (temperature-based) during the first N tokens of a session to avoid deterministic collapse to the exact same expert indices. Tunable per-customer.
3) Early-prefix normalization: during the first K tokens, apply a small normalization of the input features to reduce delimiter-driven stickiness. (This is lightweight and can be toggled per-route.)
4) Runtime backpressure routing: if an expert's queue depth exceeds threshold, dynamically route to next-best experts (even if slightly lower gating score). This trades a small quality delta for lower variance.

Medium-term mitigations / platform changes:
- Topology-aware anti-colocation: distribute likely-hot experts across NUMA/NVLink islands so a single hotspot won't saturate SMs on one device. Requires model shard placement changes at load time.
- Hot-expert replication: maintain mirrored lightweight copies of hot expert weights (quantized) to spread immediate bursts across devices. More complex but reduces single-device hotspots.
- Gating-aware tokenizer retraining: for new model onboarding, analyze tokenizer->gating correlations and consider small tokenizer tweaks or gated-finetune to desensitize gating from frequent delimiters.

Experiment plan and metrics to track:
- Primary metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, per-expert enqueue/dequeue rate, kernel duration variance, PCIe throughput, pagefault count (per node), model quality delta (perplexity or small eval set).
- Schedules: A/B run of randomized gate jitter on 10% traffic for 48h; prefetch-on-route pilot on dedicated canary pool for 24h with synthetic increased TTL; topology anti-colocation run on staging with 2 replica strategies.

Open questions and risks:
- Quality impact of randomized gating jitter is unknown for adversarial/structured prompts. Need to run small evals to detect hallucination or scoring regressions.
- Prefetch increases steady memory usage; on dense packing this may reduce total capacity. Prefetch policy must be conservative and per-route.
- Replication adds complexity to consistency when experts are updated during rollouts.

Logs and reproducible commands (dev harness):
- Replayer invocation: ./replayer --trace-id anonymized-202410 --scale 2 --preserve-tokenization --endpoint canary-moe-1 --nvtx
- Lightweight per-expert counters: use runtime flag --enable-expert-counters and fetch /metrics/expert_load?range=60s
- Kernel annotation: export NVTX=1; run with collect-kernels.sh to produce annotated perf.json for FlameGraph inspection.

Next steps (owner assignments):
- Implement prefetch-on-route prototype (Aisha, Marco) — target: config flag and safe default thresholds by 2024-11-14.
- Small eval harness for randomized-gate-jitter (Rina) — publish quality delta report within 1 week.
- Topology placement simulation (Evan) — run simulation on staging and propose anti-colocation strategy by end of month.

Notes-to-self / loose thoughts:
- This feels like a classic "content bias -> resource thrash" pattern; there's likely a cheap win in the prefetching and small randomized jitter before any heavy model or infra work.
- Add an alert that correlates pagefault spikes with p99 so operators can triage earlier.

Appendix: example short trace (sanitized)
- Request id: r-20241103-xy
- Context length: 10,928 tokens
- Observed: expert-42 enqueue 128k tokens in 800ms, pagefaults: 12, PCIe out: 58GB/s peak, p99 latency: 3.1s (baseline 0.9s)
- Kernel timeline: router(12ms) -> kv-fetch(102ms, pagefaults) -> ffn(73ms) -> attn(46ms) -> ffn(95ms) -> writeback(18ms)

If you have other production traces (anonymized) with repeated delimiter-heavy prefixes, drop them into the replayer; those are highest-value for reproducing.

End of note.
